glossary.definition: Consecutive microcycles with progressively demanding training, commonly through increased loading, volume or both.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 15 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A microcycle of substantially reduced training demands intended to reduce fatigue while retaining useful adaptations; different from the final competition taper.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 15; pp. 151–154 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: An organized sequence of microcycles pursuing a distinct adaptation, commonly including an accumulation phase and a deload.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 16 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: One or more mesocycles united by a main training purpose. A block is defined by function rather than a fixed calendar duration.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 16 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: An ordered series of training blocks pursuing a larger performance goal, often culminating in competition and including recovery afterward.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 16 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Maximal ability to produce force. The expression of that ability depends on the task, technique and current state.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 17 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Maximal force-producing capacity expressed in a specified movement; the limiting portion constrains successful full-task performance.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 17 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Increase in muscle size. In the source’s powerlifting framework, a hypertrophy block develops relevant muscle and work capacity, or helps retain muscle during a cut.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 17–18 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Training to express available muscle and general strength in maximal regulation lifts. It includes specific heavy practice and ends with a taper.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 18; pp. 290–292 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A low-demand training phase, usually after a major cycle or competition, intended to reduce accumulated fatigue and prepare another productive cycle. It has no accumulation phase.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 18; pp. 154–156 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment. Sufficient training disrupts it and initiates processes of recovery and adaptation.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 18 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Logical sequencing of training variables toward desired adaptations, manageable fatigue and performance at a chosen time.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 19 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Available range of motion at one or several joints. It is one contributor to mobility, not equivalent to loaded movement control.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 19 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Organization of body positions and movements to complete the task effectively and with controlled execution. Details can differ among body proportions.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 19 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: The source’s intersection of flexibility, strength and technique: being able to achieve and control the positions required by a task.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 19–20 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Training the systems that underlie the desired task. It ranges from broad supporting capacities to narrow competition execution.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 26–29 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: The degree to which training modes support or interfere with each other, including competing demands for recovery, time and adaptation.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 29–39 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Consistent, sequential exposure to a related stimulus for long enough to develop and retain the intended capacity.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 40–42 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A sufficient relevant stimulus together with demands that progressively exceed recent experience as adaptation occurs. It does not require every consecutive session to be harder.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 72–74 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: The highest context-dependent training volume recoverable enough to benefit from. It changes with exercise, loading, effort, recovery and training status.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 76–78; pp. 121–133 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Training-related disturbance that persists across exposures and can impair performance or adaptation when not periodically reduced. The book groups several physiological contributors.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 104–116 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: An intentionally temporary stimulus-recovery mismatch followed by sufficient lower-demand training, intended to realize a benefit after recovery. Not the same as chronic regression.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 116–118 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A conceptual description of how training perturbs function, recovery restores it and adaptation can improve it. The processes overlap and differ among systems.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 186–209 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Strategic alteration of relevant training variables to manage staleness and target needs while respecting specificity and directed adaptation.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 243–254 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Diminishing responsiveness to a repeatedly applied stimulus in the book’s model; related to, but not identical with, unrecovered fatigue.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 244–252 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Sequencing phases so retained adaptations from an earlier phase support the gains or expression of a later phase.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 278–286 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Loss of an adaptation when relevant stimulus is absent or insufficient. Maintenance can require less work than development but still needs consideration across phases.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 282–285 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Final reduction of training demands before competition to decrease fatigue while retaining muscle, strength and maximal-lift execution.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 292–299 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Evidence-informed adjustment of planned training to the observed response while preserving the objective and larger schedule. It differs from random daily training.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 156–160; p. 368 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Differences in training response between people or within the same person over time, usually accommodated by dose, progression, selection, technique and emphasis.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 308–317 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A coordinated nutrition and training phase intended to increase muscle mass; the source associates it with higher-volume work and a caloric surplus.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 16–17 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A nutritional phase aiming to keep body mass broadly stable, compatible with different training goals.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 17 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A coordinated phase aiming to reduce fat while preserving muscle. In the source, a caloric deficit can reduce recoverable training demands.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 17 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A block emphasizing improved force-producing capacity with substantial compound loading and sufficient work to retain muscle.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 18; pp. 289–290 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Time allocated to accumulation compared with deloading. A 3:1 pattern means three time units of accumulation for one of deload, not a universal calendar requirement.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, p. 16; pp. 158–160 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: The greatest load completed for one repetition of the specified lift under the stated execution conditions. Percentage comparisons require a relevant, positive reference.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 18, 82–84 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Rate of mechanical work. For force along the movement direction, instantaneous power is force × velocity; maximal lifting intent does not guarantee high bar velocity.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 35–36, 89–90 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates; coordination within and between muscles contributes to the target movement.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 32, 45–46 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Stored carbohydrate, including muscle and liver stores. The source emphasizes muscle glycogen in repeated demanding work and its restoration during recovery.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 105–107 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: A rate describing the fraction of a protein pool synthesized over time. The source overlays it with its muscle SRA model; synthesis alone does not measure net muscle gain.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 192–194 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: The angle of muscle fibers relative to their tendon. The source discusses exercise-related architecture as one contributor to task-specific force production.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 45, 193 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

glossary.definition: Capacity to perform the required training workload. It constrains MRV together with recovery capacity and is not interchangeable with general endurance.
glossary.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 128–130 (printed page labels and 1-based PDF pages coincide; 0-based PDF index is label minus 1).

interactions.title: Volume-load laboratory
interactions.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 12–14 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).
interactions.objective: Compare the arithmetic of sets, repetitions and load.
interactions.rationale: Inputs: sets, repetitions, external mass in kg. Output: sets × repetitions × kg, reported as kg·repetitions. Change one input at a time.
interactions.assumptions: Same lift, lifter and range of motion; mass proxy only. This does not estimate biological stimulus, calories, fatigue or injury risk. Positive finite inputs; reset restores the example.
interactions.staticAlternative: 4 sets × 5 repetitions × 100 kg = 2,000 kg·repetitions. Halving load halves this proxy if everything else stays fixed.
interactions.verification: Verified by direct multiplication: 4 × 5 × 100 = 2,000; 2 × 5 × 100 = 1,000; doubling any one factor doubles the output.

interactions.title: Percentage is a reference
interactions.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 78–86 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).
interactions.objective: Calculate percentage loading without confusing it with failure proximity.
interactions.rationale: Inputs: external load and measured reference 1RM, both kg. Output: 100 × load / reference 1RM (%). Adjust either value and inspect the ratio.
interactions.assumptions: Reference 1RM must be positive and relevant to the same lift. The result does not predict available repetitions, prescribe a safe weight or measure readiness. The source’s “relative intensity” names failure proximity instead.
interactions.staticAlternative: 120 kg / 160 kg × 100 = 75%. The number changes when the reference changes, even if the bar stays at 120 kg.
interactions.verification: Verified with ratios: 120/160 = 0.75; equal load and reference yield 100%; zero reference is invalid.

interactions.title: Connect the training phases
interactions.source: Scientific Principles of Strength Training, pp. 278–291 (printed page labels; PDF page index is label minus 1).
interactions.objective: Explain which adaptation each phase develops and what it should preserve.
interactions.rationale: Select each named phase and compare its role with the book’s muscle → strength → peaking → active-rest sequence.
interactions.assumptions: A conceptual ordering exercise for a competition macrocycle. Multiple real schedules can work; no kilogram gains or ideal dates are predicted. Reset returns to the example.
interactions.staticAlternative: Muscle development supports force development; force development supports maximal-lift expression; lower-demand active rest prepares another cycle.
interactions.verification: Checked against the source’s phase-order argument, preservation goals and summary tables, pp. 278–306 and 337–343.

steps.description: Develop force-producing capacity while retaining useful muscle.

title: Scientific Principles of Strength Training
subtitle: Understand the principles. Build the reasoning.
description: An independently written, source-attributed course on all eleven substantive chapters: training language, seven priorities, complete-cycle planning and evaluating powerlifting claims. Examples are educational models, not personalized prescriptions.
